title: How lovely (Psalm 84)
hook: even the sparrow finds a home near your altar; a day in your courts is better than a thousand
carry: even the sparrow has a home
tomorrow: teach us to number our days

segments.voice: Yesterday, David in the dry land, and nephesh, a word for soul that also means throat. Your line was thirsty for God. How did that first slow sip taste? Day four hundred twenty-seven.

Look up in an old train station, a barn, a covered market, and there's often a nest tucked on a beam where nobody can reach it. The building was made for trains or cows or fruit. The birds didn't ask. They just moved in, and nobody threw them out. Now go back to the temple in Jerusalem. Pilgrims arrive dusty from the road. Priests move between the altars. Smoke rises. And up in the stonework, little birds are building nests and raising chicks, right next to the holiest place in the land. One pilgrim noticed, and envied them. Today, his song.
screen: `A NEST ON A STATION BEAM.` → `BIRDS IN THE TEMPLE.` → `A PILGRIM'S ENVY.`

segments.voice: Psalm eighty-four begins, in the King James Bible: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" In King James English, amiable meant lovely, lovable. The Hebrew word is close to beloved. This is a love song for a place. Then verse three: "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars." The Hebrew word for sparrow is a general word for any small bird. The point is how small. The least important creature in the courtyard gets to live where the pilgrim can only visit. Then the road. Those who travel to God's house, verse six says, pass through the valley of Baca, and make it a well. Nobody is sure what Baca means. It may be weeping, or a kind of tree that grows in dry places. Either way, the pilgrims turn a hard valley into springs as they walk through. And then the line people remember: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness." One more detail. The heading gives this psalm to the sons of Korah. Their ancestor Korah led a rebellion against Moses, and the book of Chronicles later lists Korah's descendants among the keepers of the gates. So the people singing that they'd rather stand at the door may have been the family whose job was the door. Brahms set this psalm in his German Requiem, and congregations still sing it as a hymn. A love song for being near.
screen: `AMIABLE: LOVELY, BELOVED` · `THE SMALLEST BIRD GETS A HOME` · `THE VALLEY BECOMES A SPRING` · `THE DOORKEEPERS SING IT` · then, large: `A DAY IN THY COURTS IS BETTER THAN A THOUSAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit somewhere peaceful. It doesn't need to be a church. A bench, a window seat, the back step, a corner of your room with the light just right. Go there if you can, or picture it. Settle in like a bird on a beam. You don't have to earn the spot. Notice what makes this place feel like home: the light, the sound, the quiet. If you pray, you can whisper the psalm's first line: How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts. If you don't, simply rest where you are welcome. The bell holds the time.
How lovely. Psalm eighty-four's love song for God's house, where even a sparrow builds its nest by the altar.

Your line: even the sparrow has a home. That's a week in the Psalms: fret not, the thirsty deer, found very much, a clean heart, a soul waiting in silence, a dry land, and today a nest by the altar. Today, make room for one small creature or one overlooked person. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 84 when they arrive at church or go on pilgrimage, and it is sung in hymn settings and in Brahms's German Requiem as "How lovely are thy dwellings."

fork.setup: you're a pilgrim walking to Jerusalem, and the road runs through the dry valley of Baca. what do the pilgrims in the psalm do?
options: make it a place of springs.
fork.reveal: verse 6: they "passing through the valley of Baca make it a well." the walkers change the valley they walk through.

original.note: Hebrew: a bird, any small bird. the King James Bible says sparrow.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty line about loving church.
what it means: a pilgrim's love song, envying the small birds who get to live by the altar.
what a scholar hears: the sons of Korah, descendants of a rebel, appear in Chronicles among the keepers of the gates, so the doorkeeper line may be their own job.
recall: to lodge, to spend the night

notes: Week-end look-back (days 421–427) is in the carry.
Hebrew yedidot (84:1) glossed as 'close to beloved'. Confirm.
Tsippor is a general word for small bird; confirm.
Baca: uncertain meaning (weeping; balsam or mulberry tree). Stated as uncertain.
Korahites as gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 9:19; 26:1, 19) and the link to 84:10's doorkeeper: offered as 'may have been'. Confirm this is a fair, widely noted connection.
Brahms, Ein deutsches Requiem, movement 4 'Wie lieblich sind deine Wohnungen' sets Psalm 84:1–2, 4. Confirm.
